173e9b59c2bd3a: The people of southern Mesopotamia who created the first known urban civilization, around 4500 BC.
1978c3b95e53ee:
The Sumerians settled in southern Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq) between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. It isn't known for certain where they came from or what language family their language belongs to — Sumerian is a "language isolate," with no known relatives.

They founded independent city-states such as Uruk, Ur, Eridu and Lagash, each with its own ruler and main temple. They are credited with inventing writing, the wheel, the first known code of laws, and the base-60 system we still use to measure time.
196ca8b59c02b8: The region between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers ("between rivers" in Greek), cradle of several of the world's first civilizations.
106b425d886612:
Mesopotamia means "land between rivers" in Greek, referring to the Tigris and the Euphrates. Its fertile soil, renewed every year by the rivers' floods, allowed for agriculture so productive that it generated food surpluses — the economic base that made the first cities possible.

Over thousands of years, the region was home to the Sumerians, Akkadians, Babylonians and Assyrians, each building on the legacy of the one before.
0c0301396794f1: The first known writing system, invented by the Sumerians using wedge-shaped marks on wet clay tablets.
19563351d23521:
Cuneiform writing ("cuneiform" comes from the Latin cuneus, "wedge") was born in Uruk around 3200 BC. Scribes pressed a reed stylus onto wet clay tablets, leaving wedge-shaped marks. The tablets were then dried in the sun or baked, some surviving intact for more than 5000 years.

It began as a system of pictograms for keeping track of grain and livestock — bookkeeping, not literature. Over time it evolved to represent sounds and express abstract ideas, poetry and laws.
1a2e3c591ccd34: One of the first and largest Sumerian cities, birthplace of writing and legendary home of King Gilgamesh.
189ade5d713fff:
According to archaeological estimates, Uruk reached between 40,000 and 80,000 inhabitants around 2900 BC — an unprecedented size for the time. It was surrounded by walls that tradition attributes to Gilgamesh himself.

It's the place where the oldest known writing tablets appear, and it gives its name to the "Uruk period," when Sumerian society went from farming villages to true cities with government, temples and division of labor.
078cd3f8dd84ca: Historical king of Uruk (around 2700 BC) turned into the legendary hero of the oldest surviving epic poem.
1684057a8a67ea:
According to Sumerian king lists, Gilgamesh was a real king of Uruk around 2700 BC. Over time his figure turned into legend, the protagonist of the Epic of Gilgamesh — considered the oldest surviving narrative literary work.

The poem tells of his friendship with Enkidu, his search for immortality after his friend's death, and an account of a great flood with notable parallels to the story of Noah, written centuries later.
0b231db29afade: Sumerian-Akkadian priestess (c. 2285–2250 BC), the first author in history known by name.
0833956ea9f027:
Enheduanna was the daughter of King Sargon of Akkad and high priestess of the moon god Nanna in the city of Ur. She wrote hymns and poems that she signed with her own name — which is why she is considered the first known author in the entire history of writing, man or woman.

Her hymns to the goddess Inanna continued to be copied and studied in scribal schools for centuries after her death.
02e9eb416b7b24: A stepped temple shaped like a truncated pyramid, the central religious building of every Sumerian city.
189dbe7769e316:
A ziggurat is a religious structure shaped like a stepped pyramid, built of mudbrick, with a temple at the top dedicated to the city's patron god. It served as the administrative, economic and religious center of the city-state.

The best known and best preserved is the Great Ziggurat of Ur, built around 2100 BC and still partly standing today in Iraq.
18c0a92f7951db: The oldest known written code of laws, about 300 years older than the famous Code of Hammurabi.
17141a325e8693:
The Code of Ur-Nammu was issued by the king of Ur of the same name around 2100–2050 BC — nearly three centuries before the more famous Code of Hammurabi. It is the oldest known written legal code.

Unlike the "law of retaliation" (an eye for an eye) that Hammurabi would later popularize, many of its penalties were financial compensation: for example, cutting off another person's foot was paid with a fine of silver, not with mutilation of the offender.
1bce822d18c39d: The base-60 number system invented by the Sumerians — the reason an hour has 60 minutes and a circle has 360 degrees.
0f8bf1e902c6c3:
The Sumerians counted in base 60 (sexagesimal) instead of base 10 like we do. 60 has the practical advantage of dividing evenly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30 — far more versatile for splitting things up than 10, which only divides evenly by 2 and 5.

That system survives today in the units you use every day: 60 seconds per minute, 60 minutes per hour, and 360 (60×6) degrees in a full circle.
1347246b9493e3: Architect, priest and the first physician in history identified by his real name (c. 2650 BC).
0ed41a0e99e8e1:
Imhotep lived in ancient Egypt around 2650 BC, during the reign of the pharaoh Djoser, whom he served as chancellor, architect and priest as well as physician. He is credited with designing the Step Pyramid of Saqqara, one of the first great stone structures in history.

Centuries after his death, the Egyptians worshipped him as a deity associated with medicine and healing. As far as we know, he is the first physician in history identified by his real name rather than by anonymous legend.
01ea606ec30ed3: Egyptian medical text (c. 1600 BC) with 48 surgical cases described through clinical observation, with almost no magic.
0b36b013df5375:
The Edwin Smith Papyrus, written around 1600 BC as a copy of an even older text, describes 48 real surgical cases, each with the same structure: examination, diagnosis and treatment (or the honest admission that the case had no cure).

It is notable because, unlike most medical texts of the ancient world, it describes cases with almost pure clinical observation, without spells or religious explanations — evidence that the "observe, record, treat" method already existed 3600 years ago. It's named after the Egyptologist who acquired it in 1862, not its original author.
0e2ccd8dd18839: Greek physician (460–370 BC) who claimed that disease has natural causes, not divine ones. Origin of "first, do no harm."
07972b586bd8da:
Hippocrates of Kos (460–370 BC) is considered the father of Western medicine. His central contribution was claiming that diseases have natural causes — imbalances of the body, climate, diet — and are not punishment from the gods.

The "Hippocratic Corpus" gathers about 60 medical texts from his school. From that tradition come the Hippocratic Oath and the principle "Primum non nocere" (first, do no harm), still cited in medical codes of ethics around the world 2400 years later.
01183567a8f44f: The most influential physician in Western history for 1400 years (129–216 AD), an unquestioned authority despite anatomical errors.
11f81c394a6094:
Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) worked as a physician to gladiators in Rome, a unique source of practical experience with wounds and real human anatomy. His writings dominated Western medicine for more than 1400 years.

Since dissecting human corpses was forbidden in his time, he dissected animals (pigs, monkeys) and assumed their anatomy applied to humans, getting more than 200 points wrong — for example, he described the human liver as having five lobes, like a pig's. His authority was so absolute that questioning him was seen as almost intellectual heresy, until Vesalius challenged him with real human dissections.
0a6fb6b9c0d488: Persian physician (980–1037), author of The Canon of Medicine, a medical textbook used in Europe until the 17th century.
1fbf6d1487de17:
Avicenna (Ibn Sina, 980–1037) wrote The Canon of Medicine, a medical encyclopedia so complete and well organized that it was the main textbook in European universities until the 17th century — more than 600 years of use.

He was part of a golden age of medicine in the medieval Islamic world, which also invented the hospital as an organized institution (with wards by type of illness and patient records), centuries before most European cities.
11b993fa7d0f24: Anatomist (1514–1564) who dissected real human corpses and corrected more than 200 of Galen's errors.
0f8b6843de202f:
Andreas Vesalius (1514–1564) took the risk of dissecting real human corpses — something viewed with suspicion by the Church of his time — instead of relying on the animal anatomy that Galen had extrapolated to humans 1400 years earlier.

He published "De humani corporis fabrica" (1543), with anatomical illustrations so precise and detailed that they exposed more than 200 errors in the anatomy Galen had described. He is considered the founder of modern anatomy.
0d52930b7fb11b: English physician (1578–1657) who mathematically proved that blood circulates in a closed system pumped by the heart.
122c526b326720:
William Harvey (1578–1657) overturned 1400 years of medical belief in one stroke: he calculated how much blood the heart pumps in an hour, and the result exceeded a person's entire body weight — so the liver couldn't possibly be constantly manufacturing new blood, as had been believed since Galen.

He published his discovery in 1628: the heart is a pump, and the same blood circulates in a closed circuit. He got there with simple math and logical reasoning, without advanced technology.
15307f1c80e19b: Dutch cloth merchant (1632–1723) with no scientific training, the first human to see bacteria with a homemade microscope.
0b79c4a65a86a3:
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (1632–1723) was a cloth merchant in Holland. He learned to grind glass lenses with exceptional precision to examine threads, and with his homemade microscopes (some with more than 270x magnification) he began looking at pond water, dental plaque and other samples.

In 1676 he saw tiny creatures moving — he called them "animalcules." He had discovered what we now call bacteria and protozoa, the first human being to see them. Neither he nor anyone else would know for almost 200 more years that some of those creatures caused disease.
14e36b3dd16fd9: English physician (1749–1823) who created the first vaccine in history, based on cowpox, in 1796.
12d8f0d068aedc:
Edward Jenner (1749–1823) tested a popular observation among farmers using the scientific method: milkmaids infected with (mild) cowpox almost never got (deadly) smallpox.

In 1796 he inoculated a boy with material from a cowpox sore and then deliberately exposed him to smallpox — the boy did not get sick. He called his technique "vaccination" (from "vacca," Latin for cow). Thanks to mass vaccination campaigns, smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 — the only human disease ever completely eliminated from the planet.
0b857a944e13bf: Hungarian physician (1818–1865) who cut maternal mortality tenfold with handwashing — and was ridiculed for it.
16bada63625904:
Ignaz Semmelweis (1818–1865) noticed that, at the Vienna General Hospital, doctors who came from performing autopsies without washing their hands to deliver babies had a ward with up to 10% maternal mortality, compared to 1–2% in the ward run by midwives.

He proposed washing hands with a chlorine solution before every delivery — mortality immediately dropped to under 1%. Even so, the medical community refused to accept it, ridiculed him, and he ended up committed to an asylum, where he died at 47. Today he is considered a pioneer of hospital hygiene.
192e643e85138c: French chemist and microbiologist (1822–1895) who disproved spontaneous generation and laid the foundations of germ theory.
0b25f571009bb3:
Louis Pasteur (1822–1895) designed "swan-neck" flasks that showed microorganisms come from the outside air, not spontaneously from matter — ending centuries of belief in spontaneous generation.

He connected what Van Leeuwenhoek had seen (microorganisms) with what caused disease: he identified the germs behind chicken cholera and developed a vaccine against rabies. His work gave rise to the germ theory of disease.
1ce6295fec5d63: German physician (1843–1910) who established the rigorous method for proving which germ causes which disease.
0f6941377803a0:
Robert Koch (1843–1910) solved a problem Pasteur had left open: how to rigorously prove that a specific germ causes a specific disease. He established four criteria (Koch's postulates) still used as the standard today.

With this method he identified the causative agents of tuberculosis (1882) and cholera (1883), diseases that killed millions without anyone knowing exactly why.
0747600db40d32: English surgeon (1827–1912) who introduced antiseptics into surgery, drastically reducing post-operative infections.
1fae65e8e47d24:
Before Joseph Lister (1827–1912), surviving surgery depended a great deal on luck — not because of the cut itself, but because of the infections afterward, which killed up to 50% of major-surgery patients in some hospitals.

Lister applied Pasteur's germ theory to the operating room: he used carbolic acid to sterilize instruments, wounds and even the air in the operating theater. Post-operative mortality dropped dramatically, laying the foundations of modern surgery.
09dfe999e1977c: British nurse (1820–1910) who used visual statistics to reform military healthcare and founded modern nursing.
135356f168431c:
Florence Nightingale (1820–1910) arrived at British military hospitals during the Crimean War and found appalling hygienic conditions. Instead of merely reporting it, she meticulously collected data and presented it in visual charts (her own version of the polar area diagram).

Her charts showed that more soldiers were dying from preventable hospital infections than from combat wounds, convincing the British government to reform military healthcare. She founded the first nursing school based on scientific principles.
0b3395e12101fc: Scottish bacteriologist (1881–1955) who discovered penicillin by accident in 1928, giving rise to antibiotics.
097fa53f18f6a8:
Alexander Fleming (1881–1955) left an unwashed culture plate of bacteria behind before going on vacation in 1928. When he came back, he noticed a mold (Penicillium) had contaminated the plate, and the bacteria near it had died.

He identified that the mold produced a substance — penicillin — able to kill bacteria without harming human cells. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain managed to mass-produce it in the 1940s, just in time for the Second World War. Penicillin and the antibiotics that followed are estimated to have saved more than 200 million lives.
1f2571dfe341e7: James Watson and Francis Crick published the double-helix model of DNA in 1953.
0de4e2d0d64430:
James Watson and Francis Crick published the model of the structure of DNA in 1953: a double helix, two intertwined strands that explained how genetic information is copied and passed on.

Their model relied crucially on "Photo 51," an X-ray diffraction image taken by Rosalind Franklin, seen without her explicit permission through a colleague. Watson, Crick and Maurice Wilkins received the Nobel Prize in 1962.
178468560b5aec: British scientist (1920–1958) whose "Photo 51" was key to discovering the structure of DNA, without receiving credit at the time.
08773dbf294168:
Rosalind Franklin (1920–1958), along with her student Raymond Gosling, took "Photo 51" — an X-ray diffraction image that turned out to be crucial for working out DNA's double-helix structure.

Watson and Crick saw the image without her explicit permission, through a colleague of hers, and used it to complete their model. Franklin received very little recognition at the time and died in 1958, before the 1962 Nobel Prize (which is not awarded posthumously). Today she is recognized as one of the scientists whose essential work was historically underrated.
0f52008fbc77d0: Mnemonic for classifying a patient's mental state in seconds: Alert, responds to Voice, responds to Pain, or Unresponsive.
09854332130a07:
AVPU is the mnemonic emergency medical personnel use to quickly classify a patient's level of responsiveness: Alert (responds on their own and is oriented), Verbal (responds to a voice or question), Pain (only responds to a painful stimulus) and Unresponsive (doesn't respond to anything).

It's deliberately fast — not a full neurological exam, but a first classification in seconds that helps decide how urgent the rest of the assessment is. Explained in more detail in the course Patient Assessment and Vital Signs.
1b1d84b1b54ccd: The core of emergency assessment: check Airway, Breathing and Circulation, in that order.
120d062c7bb071:
ABC is the classic sequence for a patient's primary assessment: A — airway clear, B — breathing present and adequate, C — circulation (pulse, visible bleeding).

For a patient showing no signs of life, current resuscitation guidelines reverse the order to C-A-B: check circulation and start chest compressions before stopping to deal with the airway, because every second without circulation matters more in that specific scenario. See Patient Assessment and Vital Signs.
19fe15c33b196b: The skin and its structures — the largest organ in the body, with three layers: epidermis, dermis and subcutaneous tissue.
13a1c7ef526d0f:
The integumentary system is made up mainly of the skin, in three layers: the epidermis (outer layer, with no blood vessels or nerves of its own), the dermis (rich in vessels, nerves and glands) and subcutaneous tissue (insulating fat).

It performs five functions: protection, temperature regulation, water balance, excretion (salts through sweat) and shock absorption. See the course Human Anatomy and Physiology.
1e940964717409: The network of glands that produces hormones — slow chemical messengers with lasting effects, unlike the nervous system's electrical signals.
1815610a88d2fe:
The endocrine system releases hormones into the blood to regulate body functions — slower than the nervous system, but with effects that can last hours or years. Its main glands: the pituitary (regulates the others), the thyroid (metabolism), the pancreas (insulin) and the adrenal glands (adrenaline, the "fight or flight" response).

See the course Human Anatomy and Physiology.
18ff67d0ed3811: The system that filters blood, regulates body fluid and adjusts pH — kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra.
1c2c90c9bf4629: A network running parallel to the circulatory system that drains excess fluid from tissues and defends the body — nodes, spleen, thymus and white blood cells.
189bbc0d765c2b:
The lymphatic system collects fluid that leaks from capillaries into tissues and returns it to circulation. Along its vessels are lymph nodes, stations where defense cells check the lymph — which is why they swell when there's a nearby infection.

The spleen filters blood and the thymus trains defense cells (T lymphocytes). See the course Human Anatomy and Physiology.
0290b050d0d136: The basic cell of the nervous system, built to receive, process and transmit electrical signals.
166da55b4871f7: The tiny gap between two neurons where the electrical signal turns into a chemical message to cross it.
111e9699175409:
The synapse is the point of contact (with a tiny gap in between) between two neurons. When the electrical signal reaches the end of the axon, it releases neurotransmitters — molecules like dopamine, serotonin, glutamate or GABA — that cross that gap and activate (or inhibit) the next neuron.

See the course How Our Brain Works.
1034008728f6da: A deep brain structure key to turning short-term experiences into long-term memories.
18b29ea969d57c:
The hippocampus is essential for memory consolidation — the process of turning short-term experiences into long-term memories, which happens largely while you sleep. That's why reviewing information before bed can help you remember it better.

See the course How Our Brain Works.
165c2f031a0719: The brain's ability to change its own structure — strengthening, weakening or creating connections — in response to experience, throughout life.
1bcf3db500b7b9:
Neuroplasticity is the biological reason repeated practice makes something easier: when two neurons fire together repeatedly, their connection gets stronger. For decades it was believed the adult brain was fixed — today we know it keeps changing throughout life.

See the course How Our Brain Works.
0470af6b4b62da: Objective measurements of how the body is functioning — pulse, breathing, blood pressure, temperature and oxygenation — that replace simple observation.
03c91d7fd11e07:
Vital signs turn "the patient looks bad" into comparable numbers: pulse (beats per minute), respiratory rate, blood pressure (systolic over diastolic), temperature and oxygen saturation.

Their real value lies in taking them several times and comparing the trend, not in a single isolated measurement. See the course Patient Assessment and Vital Signs.
03c5c593ff6a4b: Precision gene-editing technology, adapted from a natural bacterial defense system, developed as a tool in 2012.
1fc6f8af6b1a94:
CRISPR is a technology that allows editing specific DNA sequences with unprecedented precision — something like "cut and paste" in the genetic code. It's adapted from a defense system certain bacteria naturally use against viruses.

Since being developed as a gene-editing tool in 2012, it's being actively researched to treat inherited genetic diseases. It also raises important ethical questions: who decides which genes get edited, and who has access to this technology?
1b6b9b3c15353c: Asking the AI to do something without giving it any prior examples — just the direct instruction.
0bd6bf4305fe89: Including several input/output examples inside the prompt so the model learns the pattern on the spot.
0c115d6fbc5f28: A technique that makes the model reason step by step before giving the final answer, reducing errors on complex tasks.
1e2af22e7881f2: An evolution of Chain-of-Thought: the model explores several reasoning paths in parallel and picks the most promising one.
0265bd707e49ca: A framework that alternates reasoning (Thought) with concrete actions (Action) and observations (Observation) in a loop.
167c04e75fd4cd:
ReAct (2022) is the framework behind most modern AI agents: the model alternates between "thinking out loud" (Thought), deciding on a concrete action (Action, like searching for information), and processing the result (Observation) — repeating the cycle until it reaches a final answer.

It reduces hallucinations because the model looks up information instead of making it up, and it's transparent: you can see the full reasoning before the answer.
1edea00c62ddb6: Using an AI to design, analyze or improve prompts that will be used with another AI (or the same one).
0b70dd5045ab04:
Meta-prompting is recursive: instead of writing the perfect prompt yourself, you ask the AI to analyze an existing prompt and improve it, or to generate several variations of a prompt for you to choose the best one — the formal technique behind this is called Automatic Prompt Engineer (APE).

The typical flow: you write a prompt → test it → identify what fails → ask the AI to improve it with that feedback → test the new version. That's exactly how production AI teams optimize their systems.
0d4b891b39d2d9: An attack where malicious instructions are inserted into data the AI will process, so it ignores its original instructions.
0a3574f807a736:
Prompt injection is one of the most important security risks when building AI applications. There are two variants: direct (the user themself tries to override the system's instructions) and indirect (an attacker hides instructions inside external data — a document, an email, a web page — that the AI will process).

The main defenses: clearly separate instructions from data, give the AI minimal privileges, and validate any action before executing it — never trust that the prompt will just "behave."
1caa88757f81d1: A parameter that controls how predictable or random a language model's response is.
1aa345370f4e78:
Temperature is the most important parameter for controlling a language model's behavior via API. At temperature 0.0 the response is practically deterministic (ideal for code or data extraction); at high temperature (0.8–1.0) responses are more varied and creative, useful for brainstorming or creative writing.

In normal chat interfaces (ChatGPT, Claude.ai) you don't control it directly — it only matters when you work with the model's API.
1160a47c3c76ba: A 5-part structure for effective prompts: Role, Context, Task, Format, Constraints.
093546b5ccaef3:
RCTFC is a mnemonic framework for not forgetting the key elements of a well-built prompt: Role (who the AI is for this task), Context (necessary background), Task (a specific, actionable instruction), Format (how you want the answer), and Constraints — what to avoid.

You don't always need all 5 elements: for simple tasks, Task + Format is usually enough. For complex or creative tasks, include them all.
03ab51a9f8d592: Using a language model to evaluate and score the quality of another model's (or its own) response.
0be8dd4a33062e:
LLM-as-Judge is an evaluation technique: instead of a person manually grading hundreds of AI responses, you ask another model (or the same one) to score each response against explicit criteria — completeness, accuracy, format, conciseness — with a brief justification.

It's the basis for how tools like LangSmith or Weights & Biases automate the evaluation of AI systems in production, though for learning, manually evaluating with a criteria framework is still very valuable.
0d42996d926361: An ethical view that judges whether an action is right based on its consequences — its most famous version is utilitarianism.
1d268cf83817fe: Immanuel Kant's ethical view: certain actions are right or wrong in themselves, regardless of the outcome.
0ee038abd4f675:
Immanuel Kant's (1724–1804) deontology holds that what's right is defined by duties and rules, not by consequences. His central test, the categorical imperative, asks whether you could want everyone to follow the same rule you're about to follow.

Another key formulation: always treat people as ends in themselves, never merely as means to your own purposes.
1c20f61ede736c: A view that asks what kind of person you want to be, rather than what rule to follow or what outcome to produce.
18bc5758d53256:
Aristotle (384–322 BC) proposed that ethics isn't about calculating outcomes or following rules, but about cultivating character. Each virtue (courage, generosity, honesty) is a middle ground between a vice of deficiency and one of excess — courage, for example, between cowardice and recklessness.

For Aristotle, virtue is learned by practicing it repeatedly, like a craft, not by memorizing definitions.
0f3634aba9960a: English mathematician (1815–1852), author of the first published algorithm intended to be run by a machine.
1d124a6a5c1bef:
Ada Lovelace (1815–1852), daughter of the poet Lord Byron, worked with Charles Babbage on his "Analytical Engine" — a mechanical computer design never built in her lifetime. In her notes on the machine, Lovelace wrote what is now considered the first published algorithm explicitly intended to be run by a machine.

She also foresaw, more than a century before real computers existed, that such machines could be used for music and art, not just numerical calculations — a remarkably forward-looking vision for her time.
18ee9b9906f55e: Polish-French physicist and chemist (1867–1934), the first person to win two Nobel Prizes in different sciences.
0a5b9f11fcf19f:
Marie Curie (1867–1934), together with her husband Pierre, discovered the elements polonium and radium, and developed the concept of radioactivity — a term she herself coined. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize (Physics, 1903) and the first person, man or woman, to win a second Nobel Prize in a different science (Chemistry, 1911).

During World War I she developed mobile X-ray units for field hospitals. She died from prolonged exposure to radiation — her own work ultimately cost her her life.
12c62575dec0a7: Austrian-American actress and inventor (1914–2000), co-inventor of a radio technology that paved the way for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
0d154cde01f207:
Hedy Lamarr (1914–2000) was a Hollywood actress during cinema's golden age, but also a self-taught inventor. During World War II, she co-developed a "frequency-hopping" system with composer George Antheil to keep radio-guided torpedoes from being jammed by the enemy.

The technology wasn't used militarily at the time, but decades later it became the conceptual basis for modern wireless technologies like Wi-Fi, GPS and Bluetooth.
073ff049f9024d: Pakistani activist (born 1997) for girls' education, the youngest person ever to receive a Nobel Prize.
136a1b5f99e9e5:
Malala Yousafzai began publicly writing about life under Taliban rule in Pakistan, defending girls' right to education, when she was barely a teenager. In 2012, at age 15, she survived being shot in the head by a Taliban gunman in retaliation for her activism.

She recovered and continued her work internationally. In 2014, at age 17, she became the youngest person ever to receive a Nobel Prize (Peace), and founded the Malala Fund for girls' education worldwide.
10eaf4572d1155: Mexican painter (1907–1954) whose deeply personal work made her an icon of art and Latin American identity.
18f569ff939b65:
Frida Kahlo (1907–1954) survived polio as a child and a severe traffic accident in her youth, which left her with chronic pain for the rest of her life. Much of her work — deeply autobiographical and symbolic — grew out of processing that physical and emotional pain, as well as her Mexican and Indigenous identity.

Although she received less recognition in her lifetime than her husband, muralist Diego Rivera, today she is one of the most recognized and influential painters of the 20th century worldwide.
198346811a5105: Guatemalan Indigenous activist (born 1959) for the rights of Indigenous peoples, 1992 Nobel Peace Prize.
1333ef48fd4d7e:
Rigoberta Menchú is a K'iche' Maya activist who internationally exposed human rights violations against Indigenous peoples during Guatemala's civil war, a conflict in which she lost several family members.

In 1992 she received the Nobel Peace Prize for her work toward ethnic-cultural reconciliation and Indigenous rights, becoming one of the most internationally recognized Indigenous voices.
00ab79b13e0608: Kenyan environmentalist and activist (1940–2011), founder of the Green Belt Movement, first African woman to win a Nobel Peace Prize.
179efa66960a34:
Wangari Maathai was the first woman from Central and East Africa to earn a doctorate. In 1977 she founded the Green Belt Movement, which has driven the planting of tens of millions of trees in Kenya, employing rural women and fighting deforestation and soil erosion.

In 2004 she became the first African woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, recognizing the link between environmental protection, democracy and women's rights.
14736823514d00:
The renal system (or urinary system) filters waste from the blood (like urea), regulates how much water and salt the body keeps, and adjusts pH through bicarbonate. The kidneys are its main organs; urine travels through the ureters to the bladder and exits through the urethra.

See the course Human Anatomy and Physiology.
